text: Convergence of MEC and DRL in Non-Terrestrial Wireless Networks: Key Innovations, Challenges, and Future Pathways

Abstract—The rapid growth in mobile communication technologies has turned mobile edge computing (MEC) into a paradigm-shifting technology that extends cloud-like capabilities and storage resources to the edge of the network. This allows computation-intensive and latency-sensitive applications to be performed in close proximity to the end-users, thereby overcoming the bottleneck issues of resource-constrained devices. However, ensuring efficient operations in MEC-empowered systems requires intelligent task execution and resource allocation across MEC servers. In particular, it underlines the main contribution of DRL in enhancing the performance of MeNT-WiNs, including autonomous aerial vehicles (AAV) and satellite communications networks. This paper investigates how DRL can meet the unique requirements of MeNT-WiNs by enhancing system efficiency, scalability, and decision-making processes across MEC architectures. First, the article reviews the fundamentals of DRL, it later discusses its integration with MeNT-WiNs and demonstrates its relevance for the optimization of satellite communications and management of AAV swarms, as well as enhancing connectivity in remote areas. I. INTRODUCTION

RTIFICIAL intelligence (AI) [1] has witnessed a significant evolution over the past two decades, transitioning from traditional machine learning (ML) frameworks [2] to more sophisticated and powerful models. Early AI systems predominantly relied on conventional ML algorithms, which were designed to discern patterns from data and perform specific tasks without the need for explicit programming. These classical ML models, such as linear regression and decision trees, were highly dependent on handcrafted feature extraction and predefined rules to function effectively. However, as the complexity of real-world tasks increased, these models struggled to capture the intricate structures and latent patterns present in raw data, highlighting their limitations and motivating the shift from ML to its subfield, deep learning (DL) [3]. In DL, the key concept is the use of neural networks (NNs) with numerous layers permitting an automated feature extraction with a hierarchical learning process. This hierarchical learning ability has made DL highly effective in solving complex problems in areas such as image or speech recognition, natural language processing (NLP), and even mastering Go and chess, all without prior domain knowledge. Because it eliminated the need for handcrafted feature generation at scale, it allowed the creation of much more flexible AI systems on top of problems that could not be solved before due to their complexity.

Building on the advancements in deep learning, reinforcement learning (RL) [4] introduced a novel approach that enables intelligent agents to interact with their environments and learn optimal strategies using the paradigm of trial and error, which enables AI to behave in such a way

as to maximize cumulative rewards over time. Therefore, it achieves great breakthroughs in areas like robotic control and strategic gameplay. Further evolution to deep RL (DRL) widened these opportunities by merging the capability provided by deep NNs with those related to making decisions based on RL scenarios. Such integration of AI models further allowed the solution and acting upon more complex unstructured problems while learning ways of navigating them; this, in turn, will significantly enhance developments in major evolving applications including non-terrestrial networks (NTNs), industrial Internet-of-Things (IIoT), smart cities, NLP, autonomous vehicles (AVs), and healthcare. DRL gives the ability to make complex decision-making autonomous for AI even in highly dynamic or uncertain scenarios. Overall, the evolution from traditional ML to DL and from RL to DRL marks the unabated improvement and extension of the problem-solving capabilities of AI. This continuing development opens up new areas in complex decision-making and improves the capability of AI systems to act more autonomously in a variety of applications.

The evolution of DRL has brought a revolution in many fields, especially in the case of mobile edge computing (MEC)- empowered non-terrestrial wireless networks (MeNT-WiNs), where its capabilities proved transformative. In MeNT-WiNs that include but are not limited to autonomous aerial vehicles (AAVs), satellite-based communication systems, and high-altitude platforms (HAPs), the use of DRL becomes relevant due to its inherently dynamic and large-scale nature. One of the critical uses of DRL in NTNs could be the optimization of autonomous satellite operations by enabling real-time decision-making of satellites for tasks such as orbit adjustment, collision avoidance, and energy-efficient trajectory planning [5]. Consequently, DRL enhances resilience and efficiency in satellite constellations by autonomously assisting with the management of complex tasks, particularly in low Earth orbit (LEO) deployments, which are integral to nextgeneration 5G and emerging 6G communication systems. In turn, within the NTN network, DRL provides crucial performance regarding the adaptive route planning of flights and aerial surveillance. Such drones often have to fly in highly dynamic and uncertain environments, whether over disaster zones or areas with very sparse infrastructure. DRL gives these platforms real-time learning and adaptation; hence, it optimizes routing and communication links to ensure reliable low-latency data transmission to ground stations. In resource management within MeNT-WiNs, DRL significantly improves spectrum and energy resource allocation for large-scale, decentralized satellite and drone networks. Given the complexity and diverse communication needs of MeNT-WiNs, DRL’s ability to learn from experience and adapt in real-time provides an effective mechanism for optimizing RF spectrum usage, mitigating interference, and ensuring fair resource allocation. In addition to this, MeNT-WiN’s cybersecurity has now begun applying DRL since highly sensitive communication channels need to be kept safe. DRL-powered systems are used to predict anomalies, attempt to block cyber-attacks, and assess network vulnerabilities, enhancing the robustness of MeNT-WiNs from threats in a time of increased digital perils. The integration of DRL into MeNT-WiNs increases not only the autonomy and performance of those networks but also opens new perspectives regarding innovative opportunities for remote sensing, environmental monitoring, and worldwide connectivity. With its autonomous resource management capability and adaptation to complex and dynamic environments, DRL surely makes MeNT-WiNs play a key role in shaping future global communications and enabling the next wave of intelligent, interconnected systems.

Traditional optimization methods face significant limitations in dealing with the complexity, scale, and dynamic nature of non-terrestrial environments. These methods often rely on static optimization techniques and predefined rules that face challenges while adapting to the highly variable conditions and diverse requirements of MeNT-WiNs. For example, resource allocation schemes based on traditional optimization algorithms are typically computationally expensive and may not effectively respond to real-time fluctuations in network demand or environmental changes. In addition, such approaches often result in suboptimal spectrum utilization, increased interference, and inequitable distribution of resources among network users, especially in decentralized systems such as satellite constellations and AAV networks. Moreover, conventional security mechanisms in nonterrestrial environments are inadequate to address evolving threats such as cyber-attacks and data breaches because they rely on predefined threat models. Similarly, traditional routing and communication strategies often fail to provide low-latency, reliable connections in dynamic scenarios such as disaster recovery or remote sensing missions, where conditions change rapidly. These limitations necessitate the adoption of more adaptive, intelligent, and scalable solutions, positioning DRL as a transformative tool for overcoming these challenges in MeNT-WiNs.

Generally, DRL serves as a transformative instrument for optimization, adaptation, and intelligent decision-making extending beyond these general application domains. It dynamically helps in the allocation of resources to accomplish energy-efficient content delivery in cloud computing (CC) for optimizing server workloads and lowering power consumption [6]. Similarly, in data centers, DRL enables the effective routing of traffic that can reduce latency while enhancing general operational efficiency [7]. In wireless communication networks, DRL ensures profound improvement in the efficiency of the spectrum, adaptive modulation, and dynamic resource allocation, hence dealing with the random traffic loads and diverse user requirements with minimum interference [8]. text: A. CC

CC has emerged as a transformative paradigm in modern computing, providing on-demand access to vast computational resources and storage without the need for direct user management. This paradigm has played a crucial role in supporting the exponential growth of mobile Internet traffic and the increasing complexity of mobile applications. The advent of mobile CC (MCC) extended these capabilities to mobile devices, enabling remote data processing and application execution at centralized cloud data centers. However, despite its advantages, MCC faces significant challenges in meeting the demands of latency-sensitive applications. The long propagation distances inherent in MCC often lead to excessive latency, which is unsuitable for real-time applications like online gaming, virtual reality, and ultrahigh-definition video streaming [11]. Additionally, the rising number of IoT devices and bandwidth-intensive services in 5G networks has further highlighted the limitations of centralized cloud architectures. Consequently, while MCC remains an important component of modern networks, it is insufficient to meet the stringent requirements of next-generation systems. As a result, there is a pressing need for architectural innovations that combine the scalability of CC with the low-latency requirements of emerging applications.

B. MEC

To address the challenges faced by the CC, the European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) proposed the concept of MEC, also referred to as multi-access edge computing. The ETSI defines MEC as a service environment where CC capabilities are integrated with information technology services at the network edge, especially within close proximity to mobile users and the radio access network (RAN). MEC decentralizes the cloud resources and moves the computing power and data storage closer to the edge of the network, hence creating an ultralow latency and a more reliable system. While MEC is integrated with the RAN, mobile traffic can bypass the traditional core network by routing data through the nearest cloud-enabled edge server. This localized cloud infrastructure reduces bottlenecks, improves base station’s (BS’s) computing performance, and reduces potential system failures [12], [13]. Through decentralized cloud services, MEC not only improves latency performance, but also expands the range of services available to consumers, enterprises, and industries, making it easier to deploy mission-critical applications. This paradigm shift opens up new value chains, unlocks diverse application scenarios in different industries, and effectively changes the future of 5G and 6G service delivery. Fig. 1 shows the basic architecture of a MEC-enabled system and demonstrates the integration of cloud services at the network edge.
C. CC Versus MEC

There exist notable differences between CC and MEC, as shown in Table II. They differ fundamentally in their architectures, operational paradigms, and application scopes. CC relies on centralized data centers, often located far from end-users, to provide scalable computing and storage resources over the Internet. While this centralized approach supports high-volume data processing and large-scale computing, it introduces significant latency and backhaul traffic due to the long distances between users and cloud servers. In contrast, MEC decentralizes these resources by integrating compute and storage capabilities directly at the network edge, closer to end-users and access points. This proximity enables MEC to deliver ultra-low latency [14], reduce network congestion, and support real-time applications that CC cannot efficiently handle, such as autonomous driving [15], augmented reality [16], and industrial automation [17]. In addition, CC typically requires robust, high-capacity core networks to handle traffic, while MEC mitigates this dependency by offloading tasks locally, resulting in more efficient network utilization. While CC excels at providing global scalability and resource availability, MEC is designed to complement it by addressing the latency-sensitive and localized processing requirements of next-generation networks, such as 5G and 6G. Together, these paradigms create a synergistic architecture that balances scalability, efficiency, and responsiveness for diverse applications.
D. Computation Offloading Models in MEC Systems

Computation offloading is a critical mechanism in MEC systems that enables resource-constrained devices to meet the stringent requirements of modern applications by leveraging edge servers. Offloading allows mobile devices to transfer computationally intensive tasks to MEC servers, alleviating their limited processing and energy resources. Depending on the characteristics of the applications and their computational demands, offloading strategies can be broadly categorized into two types: binary offloading and partial offloading. These models differ in their task partitioning granularity, complexity, and ability to handle dependencies between task components. In the following sections, we explore these models in detail, highlighting their key features, use cases, and underlying frameworks.

1) Binary Offloading: Binary offloading is a computation task model tailored for scenarios where tasks cannot be partitioned and must be executed entirely at a single location. Specifically, such tasks are executed either locally on the mobile device or fully offloaded to a MEC server. The model represents tasks using a three-field notation X (M ; τ ; N ), which captures the input data size M (in bits), the completion deadline τ (in seconds), and the computational workload N (in central processing unit (CPU) cycles per bit). These parameters characterize the computational and communication demands of applications and facilitate a straightforward evaluation of latency and energy consumption. The task is required to meet a strict deadline, ensuring completion within τ . However, this model can be extended to accommodate soft deadlines, permitting a small fraction of tasks to be completed after τ . In this scenario, the computational workload N is modeled as a random variable. Binary offloading, although simple, is widely used in the literature due to its ability to effectively model highly integrated or atomic tasks while maintaining mathematical tractability.

2) Partial Offloading: Partial offloading, in contrast to binary offloading, is designed for applications composed of multiple procedures or components, enabling a fine-grained division of computational tasks. In this approach, a program can be partitioned into two segments: one executed locally on the mobile device and the other offloaded to the MEC server. The simplest representation of partial offloading is the data-partition model, where input data bits are assumed to be independent and divisible into separate groups for parallel execution across different entities in the MEC system.

However, real-world applications often exhibit dependencies among procedures, significantly influencing the execution and offloading process. For instance, the outputs of certain components may serve as inputs for others, mandating a particular order of execution. Additionally, some functions may be restricted to local execution due to software or hardware constraints, such as image display routines. To address these complexities, a more sophisticated task model called the task-call graph, is employed, which is represented as a directed acyclic graph K(V;D), the vertices V denote distinct procedures, while the edges D denote their dependencies. The task-call graph supports three typical dependency models– sequential, parallel, and general–and accommodates detailed specifications for computational workloads, resource requirements, and input/output data for each procedure. E. MeNT-WiN Architecture

Generally, MeNT-WiNs represent the seamless integration of MEC with NTN platforms, including satellites (e.g., LEO and geosynchronous equatorial orbit (GEO)), HAPs, and AAVs. This architecture facilitates distributed computing and low-latency processing, bringing computational and storage capabilities closer to end-users, even in remote or underserved

areas. The MeNT-WiN architecture comprises several key components. Non-terrestrial platforms act as mobile edge nodes, hosting MEC servers to perform local computation, caching, and analytics. Ground stations and the core network provide backhaul support and coordinate with terrestrial infrastructure, while user equipment (UE), such as IoT devices, mobile sensors, and smartphones, interfaces with the network. Critical features of this architecture include real-time resource allocation for efficient spectrum and power utilization, task offloading from resource-constrained UEs to MEC-enabled platforms, and adaptive network reconfiguration to maintain performance under dynamic conditions such as mobility, interference, and varying link quality. MeNT-WiNs are poised to play a key role in next-generation wireless networks, with immense potential for applications such as disaster recovery, environmental monitoring, remote sensing, and enabling global connectivity. Fig. 2 presents an illustration of a MECempowered NTN environment.

The rapid evolution of wireless networks toward 6G systems demands transformative architectures capable of delivering ultra-reliable, low-latency, and ubiquitous connectivity. Traditional terrestrial infrastructures often face significant limitations in remote, rural, or disaster-prone areas due to coverage gaps, backhaul constraints, and scalability issues. In this context, MeNT-WiNs have emerged as a promising paradigm to overcome these challenges by integrating MEC capabilities with NTNs, such as satellites, HAPs, and AAVs. This integration facilitates distributed intelligence, proximity-based computation, and agile service provisioning. By enabling edge processing at non-terrestrial platforms, MeNT-WiNs significantly reduce communication latency, alleviate core network congestion, and support real-time decision-making for delaysensitive and bandwidth-intensive applications. Furthermore, MeNT-WiNs are envisioned as foundational enablers for a wide array of emerging use cases, including global IoT connectivity, disaster recovery, precision agriculture, remote sensing, and environmental monitoring. These capabilities make MeNT-WiNs a critical component in shaping the future of sustainable, inclusive, and intelligent wireless ecosystems.

F. Challenges Associated With MeNT-WiNs

While NTNs assisted by MEC (or MeNT-WiNs) are promising technologies for the next generations of 6G communications, they also face certain challenges owing to specific mobility and propagation scenarios [19], [20]. Evidently, one of the greatest needs is the optimal spectrum-sharing strategy that should prevent interference between terrestrial and nonterrestrial users, especially in cases of overlapping frequency bands. Moreover, with the integration of MeNT-WiNs into terrestrial systems, efficient management of shared spectrum is essential in order to maintain network performance and avoid interference issues. Furthermore, the significant path loss in MeNT-WiNs, especially for satellite and HAP communications, makes higher power demand inevitable to ensure reliable signal transmission. This also poses a serious concern on EE [21] issues, particularly when satellites and AAVs have power-constrained devices.

Similarly, other challenges imposed on MeNT-WiNs include latency [22], resource constraints [23], and variability within networks [24], [25]. High latency is inherent in NTNs, especially for satellite-based systems such as LEO satellites and HAPs, as the distances are long. Dynamic network topologies from mobile platforms like LEO satellites and HAPs further complicate service reliability. In these platforms, there are also severe resource limitations, with confined processing power and energy to support computationally intensive MEC applications. Moreover, security and privacy concerns are heightened by the wide geographic reach of NTNs, increasing their vulnerability to eavesdropping and cyberattacks [26]. Furthermore, seamless integration between terrestrial and nonterrestrial systems is essential for service continuity. However, it presents challenges due to differences in communication protocols and infrastructure requirements. This is an important challenge to address to realize the full potential of MeNT-WiNs in applications such as global IoT, smart agriculture, and disaster management.
G. Limitations of Traditional Optimization Methods in MeNT-WiNs
In the following, we discuss the key challenges posed by conventional optimization methods, particularly highlighting their inadequacies in dealing with the dynamic and complex nature of MeNT-WiNs.

With MEC, there exists a good, robust infrastructure to cope with the high computing requirements of contemporary applications. On the other hand, an inherently dynamic and distributed architecture, as in the MEC system, has incurred several intricacies in comparison to the classic optimization techniques, which have had difficulty staying effective in this environment. Classic approaches, such as convex optimization and heuristics, depend extremely on fixed mathematical frameworks and thus require in advance, static assumptions about the network conditions. While such approaches might suffice in controlled and stable environments, they are generally not rich enough to capture the highly dynamic and heterogeneous nature of MEC ecosystems, especially that of MeNT-WiNs. The unpredictable nature of variability in network topology, user mobility, and available resources in such scenarios worsens the problems with these traditional methods.

There are quite a few more challenges in MeNT-WiNs due to the implication of rapidly changing non-terrestrial communication environments. Variability in network topology happens quite frequently, and resource availability, as well as user mobility, go up to very high levels with LEO satellites or drones (or HAPs), making it completely inappropriate to rely on classical optimization techniques alone to meet the real-time demands. Moreover, most such approaches rely on off-line optimization procedures where the computation is performed with assumed known parameters rather than adapting to evolving conditions on the fly. In addition, classical methods often have scalability problems. Since MeNT-WiNs typically involve a vast number of interconnected devices and nodes, some standard algorithms may break down under increased computational complexity and delay, making them quite inefficient for large-scale deployments. This is complicated by the fact that one must account for links both on the ground and in space while also accounting for latency, bandwidth, and connectivity differences in such environments. Consequently, this poses a critical limitation on these approaches, as they do not handle stochastic or uncertain environments effectively. MeNT-WiNs are highly sensitive to environmental contexts, like weather conditions, which can very easily degrade the quality of the signal as well as its connectivity. These methods do not offer the degrees of adaptation to uncertainties that would be needed without much re-calibration since they are based on classic optimization algorithms designed for deterministic environments.
H. Role of DRL in MeNT-WiNs

This subsection presents the pivotal role of DRL in MeNT-WiNs. Generally, for a resource allocation scenario, real-time management is the central issue of wireless communication systems. The traditional approach to optimization usually falls short in its ability to adapt quickly to changes in the demand of users, availability of resources, or traffic loads in the network, and therefore, an optimal performance could be suboptimal. For example, the resource allocation practices based on historical trends might have caused inefficiencies where there was an unexpected change in the network conditions. In contrast to this, DRL techniques are excellent in dynamic environments as they exploit their interaction ability with the environment in real-time at all times, as DRL methods support adaptive learning, that support continuous optimization of resources [27], [28], [29], [30]. Specifically, in the case of MeNT-WiNs, arise optimization problems due to user mobility, long-distance transmission, and time-varying propagation conditions for which traditional techniques lack tractability.

DRL when integrated with MEC will make for a formidable solution for the difficulties of the NT-WiNs as this will then provide real-time dynamic resource allocation, spectrum sharing, and interference mitigation between terrestrial and non-terrestrial users. Because DRL is an always-learning mechanism, adjustments can be made in real-time regarding changes in environments hence enabling faster data transfer within the network to reduce latency. As an illustration, the DRL can optimize handovers of satellites along with routing data on AAVs for connectivity to be established in rural localities, while the DRL can maintain computational loads on edge satellites and ground stations to process data more quickly. The DRL will therefore anticipate how the network would behave and adapt based on changes in conditions for designing energy-efficient communication protocols to meet the energies at the node level. This will also enable DRL to shape optimal spectrum-sharing strategies that can not only mitigate interference but also ensure there is harmonious coexistence between these users on both the ground and in the air without compromising network performance.

I. Different Perspectives of DRL-Empowered MEC

The rapid growth of IoT devices connected over the Internet has led to the generation of massive datasets, including various media types such as audio, images, and video. Given that this data is produced at the edge of the network, it is advantageous to analyze it locally. Techniques like ML, DL, RL, and DRL are essential for efficient data analysis, quick feature extraction, and learning patterns. Moreover, proper scheduling and offloading tasks to edge computing resources are crucial for effective data processing, ensuring specific data requirements like quality-of-experience (QoE), privacy, and low latency are met. DRL techniques offer robust data prediction capabilities, making them suitable for accurately forecasting data requirements and determining which MEC nodes are best suited for processing. Below, we explore various use cases of DRL-enhanced MEC from multiple perspectives.

1) DRL-Empowered MEC From Service Providers Perspective: Bringing DRL models to the edge of the network offers several advantages for stakeholders and service providers. Processing data at the edge, where consumers or nodes generate it, reduces latency and minimizes the costs of transmitting it to remote cloud servers for analysis. This approach is beneficial across various domains such as safety, security, and marketing, including applications like fire monitoring and user segmentation. Moreover, service providers can optimize their long-term profitability by offering computational resources to end-users. For example, in [31], the authors introduced a public blockchain application within MEC, aimed at maximizing the long-term profit of service providers. In this context, miners offload their proof-of-work tasks to MEC-operated BSs, and RL-aided frameworks allow service providers to dynamically adjust prices per unit hash rate while considering miners’ highest affordable price during the mining process. The framework also allows miners to efficiently optimize their strategies.

2) DRL-Empowered MEC From Networking Perspective: From a networking standpoint, DRL-enhanced MEC focuses on integrating DRL techniques within MEC systems to optimize networking technologies. These technologies include network slicing [56], [57], network function virtualization (NFV) [58], [59], software-defined networking (SDN) [32], [33], content caching [60], [61], network privacy [62], [63], and mobility management [64], [65].

Network slicing, which decouples the physical network infrastructure into several logical networks [36], allows for more efficient use of resources. In NFV, which is a virtualization technology to manage networking functions in software, the hardware costs are reduced, and efficient service orchestration is ensured [34]. NFV enables functions such as traffic analysis and security threat detection [35], and these services run through sequences of service function chains, or virtual network functions [66]. Although NFV presents several advantages, challenges arise, particularly in resource allocation within MEC systems. Offloading and scheduling service function chains efficiently are crucial, as virtual network function execution requires specific sequences. Several works have explored these challenges, including [67], which provided an overview of resource allocation challenges, and [68], which proposed a DRL-aided strategy for service function chain scheduling.

This improves network scalability and efficiency while simplifying management tasks. The integration of NFV with SDN in MEC networks has been explored in several studies, such as LightMANO [71], which presents a lightweight platform for managing network services across distributed NFV systems. Other research focuses on the convergence of SDN, network slicing, MEC in 5G networks [72], and the fusion of MEC and cloud RAN [73]. For example, a DRL-aided approach for task offloading in mobile augmented reality applications is discussed in [38]. [46] provided an extensive survey emphasizing the DRL applications in wireless communications and networking, underscoring its potential to optimize network performance and adaptability. Furthermore, the survey in [50] investigated ML-based edge caching, presenting an ML taxonomy and content delivery strategies. Although the authors offered a holistic perspective on the role of ML in cache-aided networks, they allocated limited space to discussing RL-based solutions. Similarly, in [51], the authors conducted an extensive survey on resource scheduling in edge computing, covering techniques such as heuristic methods, approximation algorithms, ML, and game theory. text: Despite significant advancements in communication technologies, the aforementioned studies have primarily focused on ML/DL-enhanced IoT or DRL-enhanced communication, with limited exploration of their applications in NTNs. Specifically, prior works rarely explore the potential of integrating MEC with DRL-empowered NTNs and hardly provide a comprehensive analysis of DRL-enhanced NTNs empowered by MEC. Traditional optimization methods used in NTNs face inherent limitations, including their inability to handle the scalability, adaptability, and real-time decision-making demands of these networks. As a result, these methods often lead to suboptimal resource allocation, inefficient spectrum utilization, and inadequate energy management–key challenges that remain unresolved in the context of NTNs. DRL has emerged as a powerful solution to address these limitations by offering unique capabilities for optimizing resource management, spectrum allocation, and security in complex and dynamic environments. Recent advances in DRL have demonstrated its ability to adapt to non-terrestrial settings, optimize multi-objective problems, and make intelligent, realtime decisions, thereby overcoming the challenges posed by traditional approaches. Motivated by these developments, this survey delves into the integration of DRL with MEC-enabled NTNs, with particular emphasis on optimizing resource allocation, enhancing EE, and improving system adaptability.

Unlike previous works that primarily focus on terrestrialcentric applications [55], this survey highlights the unique challenges and opportunities associated with DRL in MeNT-WiNs, such as satellite communications and HAPs. It also addresses a critical gap in the existing literature by exploring innovative approaches to integrate DRL within MeNT-WiNs, particularly how DRL can transform resource management, spectrum efficiency, and energy consumption in non-terrestrial environments. By focusing on these aspects, this survey provides a broader and more comprehensive perspective on DRL applications in MeNT-WiNs. A comparative analysis of this survey with existing works is provided in Table IV, highlighting its contribution to filling the research gap in DRLassisted MEC-enabled NTN networks and paving the way for future innovations in next-generation wireless networks.
K. Key Contributions

In this article, we present a state-of-the-art survey focusing specifically on the applications of DRL in MeNT-WiN. This comprehensive survey offers a focused examination of DRL’s transformative role in NTNs, filling a critical gap in the existing literature and paving the way for future innovations in this rapidly evolving field. Accordingly, our key contributions are summarized as follows:

list_items: • We establish a structured framework that systematically explores the applications of DRL within the context of MEC-empowered NT-WiNs (or MeNT-WiNs), examining its impact on optimizing resource management, communication efficiency, and decision-making processes in satellite communication and AAV-based networks.

• The survey provides an in-depth exploration of the foundational principles of DRL, offering a clear understanding of the essential concepts governing its application in NTNs, particularly in enhancing the adaptability and efficiency of these dynamic, and decentralized environments.

• We thoroughly examine the integration of DRL into MeNT-WiNs, showcasing its effectiveness in optimizing satellite systems, improving AAV network performance, and enabling advanced decision-making in challenging, high-mobility, and high-latency environments characteristic of MeNT-WiNs.

We present and discuss the unique challenges faced while applying DRL in MeNT-WiNs, including scalability, computational complexity, robust performance, and energy-efficient communication. Additionally, we identify emerging trends and outline future research directions, providing a roadmap for advancing the field of DRL in MeNT-WiNs and guiding future developments in 6G communications and beyond.

text: B. ML

As a subfield of AI, ML, aims to design algorithms that enable systems to learn from data and improve performance over time without being explicitly programmed. ML’s strength lies in identifying patterns, making predictions, and extracting insights from data, thus allowing systems to adapt dynamically to new information [101], [2]. This iterative learning process makes ML particularly effective across various domains, such as healthcare, where it assists in diagnostics and personalized treatment plans [102], and finance, where it plays a key role in risk assessment and fraud detection [103]. Furthermore, ML powers image and speech recognition [104], [105], and recommendation systems, enhancing user experience across digital platforms [106]. Below, we discuss two types of ML models.

1) Supervised Learning: In supervised learning, a data set, containing features (or inputs) and the corresponding outputs, is supplied to the model for training, thereby called supervised learning. The model is trained over several iterations to learn how to map given inputs to outputs. The model uses the given labeled outputs to improve its performance by conducting a comparison between the actual and predicted output [107]. Supervised learning is further classified as, i) regression, and ii) classification. The regression analysis examines the relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables using a statistical method. This method minimizes the error between expected and actual outputs to derive the functional mapping between inputs and outputs. Furthermore, the output label in the case of regression can assume continuous values [108]. On the other hand, in classification, the given output labels
represent distinct classes defined in image classification, etc [109].

Typically, classification problems are addressed by employing probabilistic classifiers to map output classes based on inputs, for instance, the naive Bayes classifier [110]. The supervised learning algorithms for the ML paradigm include linear regression [111], logistic regression [112], support vector machine (SVM) [113], Naive Bayes model [110], and decision tree [114]. Similarly, the supervised learning algorithms for the DL paradigm include perceptron [115], multi-layer perceptron (MLP) or fully connected NNs (FNNs) [116], extreme learning machine [117], deep residual network (DRN) [118], connected NNs [119], deconvolutional network [120], probabilistic NNs [121], recurrent NNs [122], [123], LSTM [124], reservoir computing [125], gated recurrent units, and transformers [126].

2) Unsupervised Learning: Unlike supervised learning, where models are trained with labeled datasets to learn a direct input-output mapping, unsupervised learning operates on datasets that contain only input features, with no associated output labels. While supervised learning aims to learn a direct mapping from inputs to known outputs, unsupervised learning seeks to discover hidden patterns, groupings, or underlying structures within the data [127]. Since the data does not come with predefined output labels, the learning objective is to identify similarities, groupings, or latent representations that describe the data distribution.

Since no labels are provided, the algorithm must analyze the input data to infer relationships or organization based on statistical properties. A key example is clustering, where the model identifies groups of similar data points based on feature similarity. Another important task is dimensionality reduction, which projects high-dimensional data into lowerdimensional representations while retaining key structural information. These unsupervised techniques are often used for data exploration, feature extraction, and as pre-processing steps in broader ML workflows.

C. Federated Learning (FL)

In FL, the training of the model occurs across multiple devices or servers holding local data without sharing the raw data itself [142]. Clients (devices) collaborate under the supervision of a central server, which aggregates locally computed updates into a global model. FL ensures data privacy and security by keeping data localized, making it particularly effective in scenarios where privacy concerns are paramount. In edge computing environments, FL models can learn global patterns while leveraging data stored locally on each device, enabling applications such as mobile edge popularity prediction [143].
D. DL

DL, another branch of AI, builds upon ML by using NNs to address complex tasks where feature extraction is challenging. DL leverages NNs to model high-dimensional data [144], as they consist of layers of interconnected nodes, called neurons, which mimic the architecture of the human brain [145]. The multiple layers within these networks allow DL to uncover intricate patterns and relationships in data. Neurons are connected via edges assigned weights, which are iteratively optimized through backpropagation algorithms [146]. The learning process in DL often involves minimizing a cost function (representing the difference between predicted and actual outputs) using optimization techniques like stochastic gradient descent (GD) [147], [148], Newton’s method [149], and GD [150], allowing the system to learn complex representations. Fig. 4 (a) presents an illustration of DL.
E. RL

RL is an experience-driven learning approach where an agent learns by interacting with an environment rather than relying on a predefined dataset. The agent receives rewards or penalties based on the actions it takes within the environment, allowing it to improve its behavior over time [151]. The environment is often modeled using the MDP [152], which offers a mathematical framework for decision-making in stochastic scenarios. The aim of RL is to discover a policy that minimizes penalties (or maximizes cumulative rewards) over a specified time horizon, based on the agent’s state. Fig. 4 (b) illustrates the basic components of an RL system.
F. DRL

DRL, first introduced in [153], merges the strengths of DL and RL, making it well-suited for complex, high-dimensional problems. While traditional RL algorithms are effective for environments with limited state and action spaces, they struggle when applied to real-world scenarios that involve continuous or high-dimensional spaces. As finding an optimal policy in such environments becomes increasingly challenging, DRL was developed to overcome this limitation by efficiently handling high-dimensional data and continuous action spaces. In DRL, the RL framework consists of a self-learning agent that maximizes long-term rewards without requiring a model of the environment. At the same time, DL, inspired by biological NNs, plays a critical role in addressing the complexities inherent in these environments, enabling the agent to extract meaningful features from large state spaces. Fig. 4 (c) illustrates the basic components of a DRL setup. DRL is particularly well-suited for tasks involving sequential decision-making [154], where the agent must make a series of decisions to optimize the expected cumulative future reward. These tasks are typically modeled as MDPs, which rely on the Markov property: the next state depends solely on the current state, and outcomes are influenced by both the agent’s actions and random factors. In the following, we discuss the MDP framework, its core principles, and its role in DRL.

H. DRL Models Classification

Based on the wide variety of DRL applications, several DRL algorithm variations have emerged, primarily distinguished by whether they rely on a predefined model or not. As a result, DRL methods are generally categorized into two main classes: model-based DRL methods and model-free DRL methods. Below we discuss these categories in detail. Fig. 6 depicts the different classes of DRL algorithms.

1) Model-Based DRL Methods: In model-based DRL methods, the agent constructs a model based on feedback obtained from the environment. This model is then used to predict the impact of actions on the states and rewards, allowing the agent to derive an optimal policy. Examples of model-based methods include AlphaZero [166], model-based RL with model-free fine-tuning (MBMF) [167], imaginationaugmented agents (I2A) [168], and monte carlo tree search (MCTS) [169]. Model-based strategies typically exhibit lower sample complexity, as they reduce the need for extensive interactions with the environment. However, if the model is inaccurate, the resulting policy may be suboptimal, leading to less precise and suboptimal outcomes.

2) Model-Free DRL Methods: In model-free DRL methods, the agents learn optimal policies by directly interacting with the environment, without structuring a model of the dynamics of the environment. These methods are further categorized into different approaches based on how they learn from the interaction.

III. DRL IN MENT-WINS

MEC is envisioned as a promising solution to address the high demand for high-throughput and low-latency applications in wireless communication networks. In the context of nonterrestrial environments such as AAVs, satellite networks, and aerial drones, MEC offers the potential to bring storage and computation capabilities closer to the edge of the network, enabling faster response times and improved user experiences. However, the effective utilization of MEC resources in NT-WiNs faces challenges due to factors like intermittent connectivity, limited bandwidth, and dynamic environmental conditions. In the recent past, DRL has gained traction as a powerful tool to address certain challenges faced by wireless communication networks, for instance, resource allocation optimization, enhancing EE, improving QoS, task offloading, addressing security concerns, and network optimization. Together with MEC, DRL can offer the opportunity to enhance the performance of wireless communication networks, specifically the NTNs.

This section provides a detailed review of existing literature on DRL-assisted MEC in NT-WiNs particularly, related to resource allocation, EE, QoS improvement, task offloading, and security and privacy. This section explains how DRL-enabled MEC can bring transformative changes to communication systems in non-terrestrial settings, unlocking new opportunities for applications and services by synthesizing insights from diverse studies.
A. Resource Allocation

In general, resource allocation is a key issue in MeNT-WiNs, where computing, storage, and communication resources have to be used efficiently to optimize network performance for diversified applications and services. Recently, DRL has been considered an attractive paradigm for dynamic resource allocation in the network edge, as it has the capability to learn and discover the optimal policies that eventually lead to optimal decision-making while interacting with the environment. This subsection highlights a review of the existing literature related to DRL-assisted resource allocation strategies in MeNT-WiNs. We look into how DRL algorithms are being implemented for effective resource allocation adaptable to dynamic network conditions, traffic patterns, and user demands with the view to maximizing resource utilization, latency minimization, and optimizing network efficiency. The following subsection synthesizes insights from studies conducted within a wide range, with the aim of presenting an extended review to understand the state-of-the-art approaches in DRL-enhanced resource allocation for MeNT-WiNs.

The authors in [193] formulated a joint optimization problem that addressed both computation offloading and resource allocation in a MEC-empowered integrated aerialterrestrial vehicular network. They modeled the problem as an MDP, which captured the stochastic nature of the environment, including the variability in user demands, communication channel conditions, and computational workloads. Using their concept of minimizing the total overhead of computation in the network, they proposed a DDQL-based solution. In the system, every vehicle corresponded to some intelligent agent that interacted with an unknown and dynamic environment to learn its best policy in an adaptive manner. The DDQL-based solution harnessed DQL to optimize primary parameters, such as offloading computation decisions and resource allocation strategies. One of the strengths of this approach is adaptability; it can effectively handle changes within the system, adapting to dynamic fluctuations in traffic patterns and resource availability as they arise in the network. In [194], the authors presented a DRL-driven architecture for a mixed-integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) problem to jointly optimize resource allocation and computation offloading in an aerial-toground (A2G) network. The proposed approach is model-free DRL, which enabled the system to learn the optimal policy in a dynamic environment by using past experience rather than relying on knowledge of the underlying system model. In the context of this work, the AAV worked as an aerial edge computing node that offloaded some computation tasks from edge IoT devices to ease up their computational burden. The goal was to find the minimum of both computation delay and energy consumption through dynamic offloading and resource allocation. The results demonstrated that the proposed scheme has much superior efficiency compared to existing methods in terms of latency reduction, enhanced energy saving, and enhanced scalability of the system.

C. QoS Improvement

Ensuring high-quality service delivery is paramount in NTNs, where factors such as latency, data rate, and reliability significantly impact user experience and application performance. MEC combined with DRL presents a promising approach to enhance QoS in such environments. In this subsection, we explore the literature on leveraging DRL techniques to improve various aspects of QoS in MeNT-WiNs. By analyzing a range of studies, we aim to provide insights into how DRLbased strategies can effectively optimize QoS metrics, leading to enhanced network performance and user satisfaction.

In [207], the authors proposed a comprehensive optimization framework designed to address both latency and EE in a MEC-empowered satellite-based IoT (SAT-IoT). The network consisted of multiple satellites, gateways, and a multitude of IoT devices, all working in tandem to support a wide range of communication and computation tasks. The core objective of this framework was to jointly optimize key parameters, including offloading decisions, user association, computing resource allocation, communication resource management, and the allocation of minimal energy at the UE level. By combining these aspects, the authors aimed to solve the overarching problem of efficient resource utilization and task execution in SAT-IoT environments. This complex optimization problem was formulated as a dynamic mixedinteger problem, which could be computationally intractable in its full form. To address this, the problem was divided into two sub-problems, simplifying the solution process without sacrificing overall performance. The authors implemented their proposed joint user association and offloading decision with an optimal resource allocation (JUAOD-ORA) algorithm and conducted extensive simulations to evaluate its performance. The results demonstrated that the algorithm significantly outperformed existing baseline methods across various metrics, including total cost, latency, and energy consumption. These findings highlight the JUAOD-ORA algorithm’s ability to efficiently balance the trade-offs between computational power and energy resources, making it a highly effective solution for SAT-IoT systems.

Task offloading, the process of migrating computationintensive tasks from mobile devices to edge servers or cloud resources, plays a crucial role in optimizing resource utilization and enhancing performance in NTNs. MEC combined with DRL offers a promising approach to dynamically manage task offloading decisions based on network conditions, user requirements, and application characteristics. In this subsection, we explore the literature on DRL-driven task offloading strategies in MeNT-WiNs. By examining various offloading policies, algorithms, and optimization techniques, we aim to gain insights into how DRL can effectively optimize task offloading decisions to improve network efficiency, reduce latency, and enhance user experience in MEC-empowered nonterrestrial environments.

E. Security and Privacy

Security and privacy are assumed to be the topmost concerns in MeNT-WiNs, where transmitting sensitive data and communication operations are prone to various kinds of threats and attacks. This section presents one of the promising frameworks that integrate MEC with DRL in view of improving security and privacy. In general, with the use of DRL algorithms, MEC systems can adaptively respond to evolving security threats and effectively mitigate privacy risks while guaranteeing efficiency in network operation. This section reviews the literature on DRL-based solutions for ensuring security and privacy in MeNT-WiNs. Specifically, it examines existing studies on how DRL techniques detect or prevent security breaches, safeguard user privacy, and ensure data transmission integrity and confidentiality in non-terrestrial environments.

A DDQL is proposed to optimize the joint SORA scheme in a VEC network, where multiple vehicle users concurrently learn how to minimize system processing delay and proceed to secrecy probability maximization. On the other hand, Consul et al. 2) Scalability: Regarding scalability, one of the primary challenges is the state-space explosion problem in DRL models [239]. As the number of devices and operational states in MeNT-WiNs grows, the dimensionality of the state and action spaces increases exponentially. This leads to higher computational requirements and prolonged convergence times for DRL algorithms. The continuously changing network environment necessitates frequent model updates, compounding the computational complexity. Additionally, the computational overhead of training and inference in DRL models, particularly those employing DNNs, can overwhelm resource-constrained platforms like satellites and AAVs. This often results in processing delays and diminished responsiveness. Communication latency between distributed MEC nodes, exacerbated by long distances and high-latency links inherent to NTNs, further hampers real-time decision-making.

Energy consumption presents another significant challenge. The intensive computational demands of DRL algorithms can rapidly deplete the limited power resources of AAVs and satellites, necessitating efficient power management strategies to ensure prolonged operation and sustained performance. DRL training can be highly energy-intensive and computationally demanding, especially when large deep neural networks are involved [235]. While offline training in data centers mitigates on-board computational costs, real-time adaptation through online or continual learning–often necessary in dynamic network environments–reintroduces significant overhead. Furthermore, DRL systems frequently encounter issues related to data sparsity and imbalance, as heterogeneous nodes in MeNT-WiNs may provide non-uniform or limited data, impairing model training and decision-making capabilities. Moreover, the highly dynamic topologies of AAVs and satellites result in continuously changing communication links and coverage areas, requiring frequent policy adaptation in real time [244]. Furthermore, intermittent connectivity due to atmospheric conditions and orbital mechanics disrupts the learning feedback loop, making consistent policy updates challenging [241]. Unlike terrestrial networks, where DRL agents can rely on stable infrastructure, MeNT-WiNs require asynchronous learning and predictive modeling to mitigate these disruptions. Another critical challenge is real-time adaptation, as rapid and unpredictable wireless channel variations necessitate near-instantaneous decision-making. Additionally, traditional DRL methods, which involve complex iterative computations, may introduce unacceptable latency. Thus, lightweight policy networks, edge-assisted DRL, or hybrid model-based/model-free approaches are required to ensure computational feasibility and responsiveness.

However, sensing-communication integration brings about significant challenges, especially in NTNs where platforms like satellites and AAVs operate in dynamic environments with resources that fluctuate. The central issue to be addressed is how to make the various trade-offs between sensing accuracy and communication performance in general, especially when both functions need to be executed in parallel.

One of the most promising avenues for future research involves the application of DRL algorithms to ISAC-enhanced MeNT-WiNs, where DRL can be instrumental in optimizing the dual functionalities of sensing and communication, enabling intelligent decision-making to balance competing demands while ensuring fairness. D. Semantic Communication in MeNT-WiNs

In non-terrestrial environments, where bandwidth is often constrained, and network conditions are highly variable, traditional methods of communication that focus on the accurate transmission of bitstreams may become inefficient. Semantic communication, which shifts the focus from transmitting raw data to conveying the underlying meaning or semantics of the information, becomes a viable solution to meet the scarcity of resources in NTNs. Specifically, in the context of MeNT-WiNs, this approach can greatly reduce transmission overhead and improve system efficiency, as only the most essential information is sent across the network, minimizing the use of limited resources [251]. Additionally, by prioritizing the transmission of the meaning (semantics) of data rather than raw data, semantic communication aligns seamlessly with the vision of intelligence as a service in 6G networks.

The integration of semantic communication into MeNT-WiNs presents three primary challenges: security, resource allocation, and multimodality [252]. In MeNT-WiNs, DRL can significantly enhance semantic communication by addressing these key challenges. It optimizes bandwidth and power usage, ensuring efficient resource utilization in constrained environments, and prioritizes data modalities based on their semantic importance and network conditions. Additionally, it strengthens security by dynamically adapting to evolving threats and assists the encoding and decoding processes by learning effective semantic representations [253]. These capabilities make DRL an essential enabler for realizing the full potential of semantic communication in MeNT-WiNs.

J. EE in DRL-Enabled MeNT-WiNs

The integration of DRL into MeNT-WiNs presents significant challenges related to energy consumption, particularly given the limited resources of platforms like AAVs, LEO satellites, and HAPs. DRL algorithms, especially those involving deep NNs, require substantial computational resources for both training and inference. The training phase, in particular, is highly energy-intensive, as DRL models must process large datasets and perform numerous iterations to update their parameters. Similarly, the inference phase, where DRL models make real-time decisions, can lead to high energy consumption, especially on platforms with constrained power budgets.

To address these energy challenges, several strategies can be implemented. Model compression techniques, such as pruning and quantization [245], can reduce the size and complexity of DRL models, thereby decreasing computational requirements and energy usage during both training and inference. Additionally, energy-aware resource allocation strategies can be employed, where DRL itself can be used to optimize the distribution of computational and communication tasks across the network, minimizing energy consumption while still meeting performance requirements. Another promising solution is offloading tasks from energy-constrained nodes (like AAVs) to more powerful edge servers or MEC nodes, which can process the data without draining the local platform’s energy reserves. Furthermore, the incorporation of FL into DRL systems reduces the need for energy-intensive data transfers by ensuring that only model updates (rather than raw data) are shared between distributed nodes [264]. These techniques enable DRL to be more energy-efficient, making it viable for large-scale deployment in resource-constrained environments like MeNT-WiNs.
K. Securing DRL-Enhanced MeNT-WiNs

While DRL offers substantial benefits in resource management and system optimization, its integration into MeNT-WiNs introduces several new security concerns that must be addressed to ensure the robustness and reliability of these networks. One of the primary risks is the vulnerability of DRL models to adversarial attacks [265], where malicious entities can manipulate the input data or training process to cause the model to make suboptimal or harmful decisions. For example, attackers could target the task offloading process in a satellite network by manipulating network traffic to force a DRL-based system into making inefficient resource allocation decisions, leading to network congestion or service degradation. Similarly, data poisoning attacks could compromise the learning process of DRL models by introducing erroneous data into the system, corrupting the trained model, and reducing the overall system reliability.

To mitigate these security threats, various solutions can be employed. Secure FL [266] is one such approach, where multiple agents collaboratively train DRL models without sharing sensitive raw data, thus preserving privacy while preventing malicious tampering. Additionally, anomaly detection systems powered by DRL [162] can continuously monitor network traffic for unusual patterns or behaviors that may indicate potential attacks, such as unauthorized access attempts or DDoS attacks. DRL can also be used to enhance adaptive security policies, dynamically adjusting encryption mechanisms, access controls, and intrusion detection protocols [267] in response to real-time network conditions or identified threats. This adaptive approach allows MeNT-WiNs to respond proactively to security challenges while maintaining high levels of performance. By integrating robust security mechanisms with DRL, MeNT-WiNs can ensure secure, efficient, and resilient operations, safeguarding sensitive data and preventing potential disruptions in non-terrestrial communication systems.
